plaudo (plōdo, Varr. ap. , and ), si, sum, 3, v. a. and n.

plānus, a, um, adj.
for placnus; root plac-; Gr. πλακοῦς; cf. 2. plaga, planca
,
even, level, flat, plane (class.; cf. aequor).
Lit.: facilis et plana via,: cum duae formae praestantes sint, ex solidis globus, ex planis circulus aut orbis, : planum et aequabile corpus universitatis,: planus et aequus locus,: litus,: carina,: pisces,flat-fish,: aedificia, quae plano pede instituuntur,on level ground,: postquam jacuit planum mare,: planā faciem contundere palmā,flat,.—Comp.: aditus planior,.— Sup.: planissimus locus,. —
Subst.: plānum, i, n., level ground, a plain: aciem in planum deducit,: per planum ire,: cadere in plano,: in planum deferre aliquid,: castra in plano erant,: de plano,on level ground,; : ad planiora,.—In partic., jurid. t. t.: e plano or de plano, on level ground, below, not on the bench, i. e. out of court, extrajudicially: aut e plano aut e quaesitoris tribunali,: custodiae non solum pro tribunali, sed et de plano audiri possunt,; .—
Trop.
Lowly, inconsiderable, humble (post-Aug.): haec magnanimitas melius in tribunali, quam in plano conspicitur,shows better in one of high than of low station,: fortunam suam in planum deferre,: de plano, without difficulty, easily (poet.): hoc tibi de plano possum promittere,.—
Plain, clear, distinct, intelligible (class.): satin' haec sunt tibi plana et certa!: narrationes,: conjectatio,: pol planum id quidem est,it is plain, clear, evident,: planum facere, to make plain, clear, or intelligible, to set forth, ; ; ; 2, 5, 64, § 165: planum facere multis testibus,: planum facere atque probare,.—
Easy, free from danger: illam viam vitae, quam ante praecipitem et lubricam esse ducebat, huic planae et stabili praeponendam esse,.—Hence, adv.: plānē, plainly, evenly; trop., simply, clearly, distinctly, intelligibly.
Lit. (class.): videre,: scribere,: scire,: plane loqui,: plane et dilucide loqui,: plane et perspicue expedire aliquid,: plane et Latine loqui,to speak plainly, right out, without circumlocution,.—Comp.: quo pacto excludi potis est planius, quam, etc.,: planius dicere (opp. dicere obscurius),: planius atque apertius dicere,: quid, hoc planius egissem, si, etc.,: ostendere,.—Sup.: apertissime planissimeque explicare,.—
Transf., wholly, entirely, completely, quite (class.), : perdidisti mulierem,: illam plane amo,: carere sensu communi,: quod reliquos coheredes convenisti, plane bene,you have acted quite right,: illud plane moleste tuli, quod, etc.,: non plane par,: ex rebus penitus perspectis, planeque cognitis,: propemodum, vel plane potius,: explicari mihi tuum consilium plane volo, ut penitus intellegam,thoroughly,: planissime perii,: plane perfecteque eruditus,: plane atque omnino rem defuisse,: plane cum,particularly as,; cf.: et plane quid rectum esset diutius cogitare malui,.—
By all means, assuredly: eo acrius te rogo ut plane ad nos advoles,—
In partic., in affirmative answers, certainly, to be sure, exactly so (anteclass.): ego et domi privatus sum et perii. Ge. Plane istuc est, ; : De. Etiam argentum est ultro objectum, ut sit, qui vivat, dum aliud aliquid flagitii conficiat Ge. Planissume, .—
Besides, but (late Lat.), ; .

la:verb:placeo.html:
plăcĕo, cŭi and cĭtus, cĭtum, 2, v. n. (
part. fut. pass.: dos placenda,; v. I. A. fin.) [cf. placo], to please, to be pleasing or agreeable, to be welcome, acceptable, to satisfy (class.).
Lit.
In gen.: ungor ut illi placeam,: meo neque cara'st cordi neque placet,: si placeo, utere,: non placet Antonio consulatus meus: at placuit P. Servilio,; : et quae vobis placita est condicio, datur. : nec dubito, quin mihi (Erigona) placitura sit,: exspecto quid illis placeat de epistolā ad Caesarem,: tibi Ne Enipeus Plus justo placeat,: dis, quibus septem placuere colles,; ; : quid placet aut odio est,: quod spiro et placeo (si placeo) tuum est,; : sibi non placere, quod (Aristides) cupide elaborasset, ut, etc.,: quis gener hic placuit censu minor,: Deo placere non possunt,.—As act.: si illa tibi placet, placenda dos quoque'st quam dat tibi,must be pleasing,.—
In partic.
In scenic lang., of players or pieces presented, to please, find favor, give satisfaction: primo actu placeo, prol. alt. 31: cui scenico placenti,; ; : populo ut placerent quas fecisset fabulas,; id. Hec. prol. alt. 12: ubi (fabulae) sunt cognitae, Placitae sunt,.—
Placere sibi, to be pleased or satisfied with one's self, to flatter one's self, to pride or plume one's self: ego numquam mihi minus quam hesterno die placui,: nolo tibi tam valde placeas,; : tu tibi tunc curruca places,: omnes competitores placebant sibi, omnes omnibus displicebant,.—
Transf.: placet mihi (tibi, etc.), or simply placet, it pleases me, it seems good, right, or proper to me; it is my opinion, I am of opinion, I hold, believe, intend, purpose; and in perf., placuit, or placitum est, it is decided, resolved, determined (mihi, nobis, etc., or absol.).
In gen.
With dat.: ut ipsi auctori hujus disciplinae placet,: ut doctissimis sapientissimisque placuit,: postea mihi placuit, ut summorum oratorum Graecas orationes explicarem,: ita nobis placitum est, ut, etc.,: sic Justitiae placitumque Parcis,: si placitum hoc Superis,.—With subject-clause: duo placet esse Carneadi genera visorum,; : sic visum Veneri, cui placet impares Formas, etc., mittere,: quis paria esse fere placuit peccata, laborant, Cum, etc.,.—
Without dat., : sed, si placet, in hunc diem hactenus,; : placitum est, ut in aprico maxime pratuli loco considerent,.—With neutr. pron. as subj.: hocine placet?.—With subj.: placuit ad hunc primum ferremus aditum,.—With subject-clause: placet enim esse quiddam in re publicā praestans et regale, etc.,; : si enim pecunias aequari non placet,: hos corripi placitum,; ; .—
In partic.
In publicists' lang., to resolve, will, order, determine: senatui placere, ut C. Pansa, etc.,: senatui placere, C. Cassium, etc.,: deliberatur de Avarico in communi concilio, incendi placeret an defendi,: quamobrem placitum est mihi, ut, etc.,, A, § 4: edixit, mulieres ante horam quintam venire in theatrum non placere,; cf.: quid placeat, die,your decision,.—
Si dis placet, please the gods; and in eccl. writers: Deo placere,; v. deus.— Hence, *
plăcens, entis, P. a., pleasing, charming, dear: expetendum esse quod non placens sit,: placens uxor,.—Acceptable: hostia placens Deo,: sibi placentes,self-willed, Pet. 2, 10.—
plăcĭtus, a, um, P. a., pleasing, agreeable, acceptable (mostly poet.): placita es simplicitate tuā,you are pleasing, you please,: oliva,: amor,: bona,: in locum ambobus placitum exercitus conveniunt,: artes,: exemplum,: eum (regem creari) quasi placitissimum diis. qui, etc.,. 3. 9 (the reading acceptissimum is a later emendation).—Abl. absol.: sic placito ocius surrexit. : placiti dies,appointed days,.—
Subst.: plăcĭtum, i, n.
Prop., that which is pleasing or agreeable: ultra placitum laudare,more than is agreeable,.—
Transf.
An opinion, sentiment (post-Aug.): Catonis placita de olivis,.—
A determination, prescription, order: medicorum placita,.—
A maxim, principle: ipse (Rubellius) placita majorum colebat,: sapientium placita,: Stoicorum,: philosophorum,: nec est quare hoc inter nostra placita mireris,: decreta, quae Graeci vocant dogmata, nobis vel decreta licet adpellare vel scita vel placita,: philosophiae placita, § 37: Babyloniorum,; .

la:verb:placo.html:
plāco, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
etym. dub.; cf.: placeo, planus
.
To reconcile; constr. alicui, aliquem (class. and freq.): agedum, fac, illa ut placetur nobis,that she be reconciled to us,: vereor ut placari possit, (cf.: redigam vos in gratiam, v. 73): coeperas eum mihi placare,: rogavit ut te sibi placarem,: his vocibus cum in se magis incitarent dictatorem quam magistro equitum placarent,: Hannibalem pater filio meo potui placare,: placare aliquem rei publicae,.—Pass.: quae fuit eorum tanta iniquitas, ut placari populo Romano non possent?: neque nullam spem habebat, patrem sibi placari posse,.—In mid. force; usually with in and acc.: numquam animo placari potuit in eum, be reconciled, i. e. consent to a reconciliation, ; cf. : homo quietus et sibi ipsi placatus,at peace with himself, tranquil,.—
In gen., to quiet, soothe, calm, assuage, appease, pacify: animos placare ac lenire,: placare et mitigare animum,: numen deorum immortalium, Caes. B.

G. 6, 15: aliquem beneficiis,: iram deorum donis,: benevolos objurgatores,: invidiam,.—Poet.: ventos sanguine,: Hippotades cum vult, aequora placet,: escā ventrem iratum,: sitim,to quench,.—

To endeavor to appease, ; .— Hence, plācātus, a, um, P. a., soothed, appeased, calmed; quiet, gentle, still, calm, peaceful (class.): animi quietus et placatus status,: tranquilla, quieta vita,: placidae ac minime turbulentae res,: maria,: vultu ac sermone in omnes placato,.—Comp.: placatiore animo aliquid facere,; : dii,.—Sup.: quies placatissima,.—Hence, adv.: plācātē, quietly, gently, calmly, composedly (class.): omnia humana placate et moderate feramus,. —Comp.: remissius et placatius ferre,.

la:adj:plenus.html:
plēnus, a, um, adj.
from the root ple-; Sanscr. prā-, to fill; Gr. πλα- in πίμπλημι, πλήθω; Lat. plerus, plebs, populus, etc.; whence compleo, expleo, suppleo
,
full, filled with any thing (class.; cf.: refertus, oppletus).
Lit.
In gen., with gen.: rimarum,: corpus suci,: Gallia est plena civium Romanorum,: domus plena caelati argenti,. § 35: vini, somni,:

stellarum, .—With abl.: plena domus ornamentis,: vita plena et conferta voluptatibus,: plenum pueris gymnasium,.—Absol.: auditorium,: plenissimis velis navigare,with swelling sails,.—As subst.: plēnum, i, n., space occupied by matter, a plenum, .—Adverb.: ad plenum, to repletion, copiously, abundantly (poet.), : hic tibi copia Manabit ad plenum benigno Ruris honorum opulenta cornu,; so : philosophiae scientiam ad plenum adeptus,.—

In partic.
Of bodily size, stout, bulky, portly, plump, corpulent (class.): pleni enective simus,: vulpecula pleno corpore,: frigus inimicum est tenui: at prodest omnibus plenis,: femina,.—Comp.: tauros palea ac feno facere pleniores,.—Sup.: plenissimus quisque,.—
Of females, big, with child, pregnant (class.): et cum te gravidam et cum te pulchre plenam aspicio, gaudeo,: femina,; : sus plena,; cf.: Telluri plenae victima plena datur (preceded by gravida),.—
Filled, satisfied (poet.), : plenus cum languet amator,sated with reading,; cf.: illa bibit sitiens lector, mea pocula plenus,.—
Full packed, laden; with abl.: quadrupedes pleni dominis armisque,: exercitus plenissimus praedā,: crura thymo plenae (apes),.—Absol.: vitis,.—
Entire, complete, full, whole: ut haberet ad praeturam gerendam plenum annum atque integrum,: gaudia,: numerus,: pleno aratro sulcare,with the whole plough sunk in the ground,: sustineas ut onus, nitendum vertice pleno est, i. e. toto,: pleno gradu,at full pace, at storming pace,.— Neutr. adverb.: in plenum, on the whole, generally (post-Aug.), ; .—
Of the voice, sonorous, full, clear, strong, loud (class.): vox grandior et plenior,: voce plenior,.—
Of letters, syllables, words, full, at full length, not contracted, unabridged: pleniores syllabae,: ut E plenissimum dicas,: siet plenum est, sit imminutum,: plenissima verba,.—
Of food and drink, strong, hearty, substantial: pleniores cibi,: vinum,.—
Full, abundant, plentiful, much: non tam Siciliam, quam inanem offenderant, quam Verrem ipsum, qui plenus decesserat,: urbes,: pecunia,much money,: mensa,.—Comp.: serius potius ad nos, dum plenior,: tres uno die a te accepi litteras, unam brevem, duas pleniores,fuller, larger,.— Sup.: plenissima villa,.—
Of age, full, advanced, ripe, mature: jam plenis nubilis annis,marriageable,: plenus vitā,: annis,full of years, that has reached extreme old age,: plenior annis,: annus vicesimus quintus coeptus pro pleno habetur,.—
Law t. t.: pleno jure, with a complete legal title: proinde pleno jure incipit, id est et in bonis et ex jure Quiritium, tua res esse,: pleno jure heres fieri, al.—
Trop., full, filled.
In gen., with gen.: plenus fidei, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 342 Vahl.): jejunitatis plenus,: consili,: viti probrique,: fraudis, sceleris, parricidi, perjuri,: offici,: negoti,full of business,; : irae,: ingenii,: laboris,: quae regio in terris nostri non plena laboris?is not full of our disaster?.—With abl.: plenus sum exspectatione de Pompeio,full of expectation,: laetitiā,: humanitate,; .—
In partic.
Complete, finished, ample, copious (class.): orator plenus atque perfectus,: plenior, opp. to jejunior,: oratio plenior,: pleniora scribere,.—
Full of, abounding or rich in any thing: plenum bonarum rerum oppidum,: quis plenior inimicorum fuit C. Mario?: pleniore ore laudare, with fuller mouth, i. e. more heartily, .—Hence, adv.: plēnē.
Lit., full (post-Aug.): vasa plene infundere,.—
Trop., fully, wholly, completely, thorougnly, largely (class.): plene cumulateque aliquid perficere,: plene perfectae munitiones,: aliquid vitare,: plene sapientes homines,: praestare aliquid,perfectly,.—Comp.: plenius facere aliquid,: alere,.—Sup.: quamvis illud plenissime, hoc restrictissime feceris,.

plebs (in inscriptions often PLEPS), -bis, and archaic plēbēs († plēbis), is and ĕi (plebium, Prud. στεφ. 10, 709:
plebibus,), f.
root ple-, fill; whence Gr. πίμπλημι, πλήρης; cf. πλῆ θος, multitude
.
Lit., the common people, the commons or commonalty, the plebeians (opp. the patricians, senators, and knights; whereas populus signifies the collective people, including, therefore, the Senate),: plebes in hoc regi antistat loco, licet Lacrumare plebi, regi honeste non licet, Enn. ap. Mign. (Trag. v. 271 Vahl.): plebs a populo eo differt quo species a genere: nam appellatione populi universi cives significantur, connumeratis etiam patriciis et senatoribus: plebis autem appellatione sine patribus et senatu ceteri cives significantur,; cf. : plebes dominandi studio permota a patribus secessit,: ita tribuni plebei creati duo,: dum decem tribunos plebi faceret,: non enim populi, sed plebis eum (sc.: tribunum plebis) magistratum esse,: populo plebique Romanae,: in duas partes ego civitatem divisam arbitror in patres, et plebem,; : Martia Roma triplex equitatu, plebe, senatu,.—
Transf., in gen.
The great mass, the multitude: in Hyrcaniā, plebs publicos alit canes, optimates domesticos,: plebem et infimam multitudinem delinire,.—
With accessory notion of contempt, the populace, the lower class or order, the mass (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): multitudo de plebe,: si quadringentis sex septem millia desunt, Plebs eris,you shall be plebeian,: misera,: ventosa,: immensa nimiaque,.—Among the gods: plebs Superūm, Fauni, Satyrique, Laresque, Fluminaque, et Nymphae, Semideūmque genus,.—Of bees, a stock, swarm, hive (meaning the great mass, opp. to the queen); in plur. (rare): tres alveorum plebes,: corona plebium, Prud. στεφ. 10, 709.—
The whole people, nation, community, = populus (late Lat.), : plebs tua Israel, et saep.
